No. Association alone does not establish causation. Outdoor temperature or season is a plausible lurking variable: when the weather is hot, sales of both products may rise. To establish causation, use a well-controlled randomized experiment that controls other factors. If an experiment is infeasible, use a rigorous quasi-experimental or causal-inference design rather than relying only on a simple correlation coefficient.

The means are $\bar{x}=287.5$ and $\bar{y}=41.5$. Let

$$S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2,\quad S_{yy}=\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2,\quad S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}).$$

a. The correlation coefficient is

$$r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}\approx-0.8074.$$

b. The slope and intercept are

$$b_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\approx-0.20973,$$

$$b_0=\bar{y}-b_1\bar{x}\approx101.7968.$$

Thus the regression equation is

$$\hat{y}=101.7968-0.20973x.$$

The data show a fairly strong negative association.
